raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a catheter-based strategy for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Its biological rationale is strong: in nonvalvular AF, most atrial thrombi arise from the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated cul-de-sac in which loss of contractility, stasis, endothelial dysfunction, and variable anatomy promote thrombogenesis [1]. The field evolved from the discontinued PLAATO system to contemporary endocardial nitinol devices, with early feasibility studies demonstrating that transseptal access, LAA sizing, device anchoring, and peri-device sealing were technically achievable [2,3].

The randomized evidence base began with WATCHMAN. PROTECT AF showed noninferiority of LAAC to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, albeit with early procedural complications [4]. Longer follow-up suggested fewer hemorrhagic strokes and lower cardiovascular mortality, while the PREVAIL trial improved procedural safety but did not meet all prespecified efficacy criteria [5-8]. Patient-level 5-year data from PROTECT AF and PREVAIL supported comparable overall stroke prevention versus warfarin, with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, and post-procedure major bleeding [9]. These trials established the central trade-off of LAAC: an upfront invasive hazard in exchange for reduced long-term exposure to anticoagulation.

Observational studies then broadened clinical experience, especially in patients considered poor candidates for long-term oral anticoagulation. ASAP suggested feasibility of WATCHMAN implantation without a warfarin transition in patients with warfarin contraindications [10]. EWOLUTION, a large real-world European registry, reported high implant success despite older, higher-risk patients and frequent deviation from trial antithrombotic protocols [11,12]. With the next-generation WATCHMAN FLX, PINNACLE FLX demonstrated high procedural success and low early complication rates in a prospective U.S. study [13]. In parallel, the U.S. NCDR LAAO Registry provided national surveillance, showing that commercial recipients were older and had greater thromboembolic and bleeding risk than pivotal-trial participants, while contemporary procedural complication rates were generally lower than in early trials [14-16].

Evidence with direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) comparators has refined patient selection. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC or DOACs and showed noninferiority for a broad composite endpoint; 4-year follow-up sustained this finding and suggested lower nonprocedural bleeding after LAAC [17,18]. Device choice has also matured. The Amulet IDE trial found the Amplatzer Amulet noninferior to WATCHMAN for safety and effectiveness and superior for anatomical occlusion, but with more procedure-related complications early in operator experience [19]. SWISS-APERO and the global Amulet observational study further emphasized that device design, landing-zone anatomy, and imaging modality influence residual leak and thrombus detection [20,21].

Recent randomized trials have expanded the debate beyond the classic “contraindication to anticoagulation” population. OPTION studied patients after AF ablation and found LAAC noninferior to anticoagulation for death, stroke, or systemic embolism while reducing nonprocedural bleeding [22]. In contrast, CLOSURE-AF, enrolling frailer high-risk patients and comparing LAAC with contemporary medical therapy, did not demonstrate noninferiority for its composite endpoint [23]. CHAMPION-AF, in anticoagulation-eligible patients, found WATCHMAN FLX noninferior to non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism and superior for nonprocedural bleeding at 3 years [24]. Taken together, these trials suggest that LAAC is not a uniform substitute for anticoagulation; net benefit depends on bleeding risk, competing mortality, procedural risk, and patient preference.

Important complications include pericardial effusion, device embolization, vascular complications, device-related thrombus (DRT), and peri-device leak. DRT is uncommon but clinically meaningful; persistent or recurrent DRT carries thromboembolic risk and usually prompts intensified antithrombotic therapy and repeat imaging [25,26]. Small peri-device leaks, once considered benign if ≤5 mm, have been associated with higher late ischemic events in long-term analyses, supporting careful procedural technique and structured surveillance [27]. Post-implant antithrombotic therapy remains heterogeneous; registry data suggest that anticoagulation without aspirin may reduce early adverse events compared with anticoagulation plus aspirin, but randomized evidence remains limited [28].

Current U.S. and European AF guidelines position percutaneous LAAC as reasonable for selected patients with AF, elevated stroke risk, and contraindications or intolerance to long-term anticoagulation, with weaker support for those at high bleeding risk who remain anticoagulation-eligible [29,30]. Future priorities include head-to-head trials in precisely phenotyped populations, standardized CT/TEE surveillance, leak and DRT management algorithms, and shared decision tools that quantify procedural risk against lifetime bleeding and thromboembolic risk.
